question_en: If a zero-coupon bond's annual YTM stated with a periodicity of 4 is 5.80%, then the annual YTM stated with a periodicity of 2 is closest to:
explanation_en: Relationship between Z-spread, OAS, and embedded option OAS = Z-spread − Option value OAS < Z-spread: Callable bond OAS > Z-spread: Putable bond The Z-spread, or zero-volatility spread, is a constant percentage that is added to the rate for each maturity in a government spot yield curve. This enhanced spot rate is used as the discount rate for a bond's cash flows and equates the present values for all cash flows to the bond's market price. Nongovernment bonds have credit risk and liquidity risk; these risks are generally not present in government bonds. The embedded options in callable or putable bonds represent an additional type of risk. The Z-spread is the additional yield required to compensate investors for all these risks, including the embedded options. To compare bonds with options to option-free bonds, the value of the option must be subtracted from the Z-spread, which results the option- adjusted spread (OAS). A putable bond's OAS is higher than its Z-spread. In this question, the putable bond's OAS is 125 basis points (bp), so its Z-spread is less than 125 bp. (Choice B) The implied put value is 125 bp higher than the Z-spread, not the government spread. (Choice C) Volatility risk relates to the value of the embedded option. Since OAS essentially separates the option risk from the other risks, OAS does not account for volatility.

The Z- spread, or zero-volatility spread, is a constant percentage that is added to each spot rate; the combined rate is then used as the discount rate for each maturity. This adjustment to each discount rate makes the theoretical price equal to the market price. For callable and putable bonds, the Z-spread includes the value of the embedded option. This means that a portion of the additional yield incorporates the option value. Subtracting that option value compensates for the other risks mentioned above. question_en: If a putable bond has an option-adjusted spread (OAS) of 125 basis points (bp), the most appropriate conclusion is that:
option_a: its zero-volatility spread is less than 125 bp.
option_b: the put option value is 125 bp higher than the bond's government spread.
option_c: the appropriate compensation for this bond's liquidity, credit, and volatility risks is 125 bp.
explanation_en: A bond's yield-to-maturity (YTM) describes and quantifies the rate of return that investors demand given its maturity and perceived credit quality. YTM is given as a percentage, and is the sum of two components: The benchmark rate, which is also known as the risk-free rate of return; and The spread, which consists of the additional amount of return over the benchmark rate. The benchmark rate applies to government bonds, which are assumed to have no risk of default and are therefore referred to as risk-free bonds. The benchmark rate incorporates macroeconomic factors such as a government's fiscal and monetary policies, expected inflation, and exchange rates for the issuer's currency (Choices B and C). The spread captures the impact of factors that are specific to the nongovernment issuer as well as the bond itself. These include the issuer's credit risk, both in absolute terms and relative to that of other issuers; liquidity of the bond; and whether the bondholder is subject to income tax on the coupon interest. All these factors are expressed as an additional percentage that compensates investors for the additional risks. A risky bond's YTM is the sum of the benchmark rate and the spread.

Relationship between Z-spread, OAS, and embedded options
OAS = Z-spread − Option value
OAS < Z-spread: Callable bond

When the cash flows of a nongovernment bond are discounted using a government bond spot rate curve, the theoretical price is usually higher
than the market price. This is due to the spot rates not accounting for the risks of the nongovernment bond (eg, credit risk, liquidity). The Z-
spread, or zero-volatility spread, is a constant percentage that is added to each spot rate; the combined rate is then used as the discount rate for

in a spread that accounts for risks other than the option; this spread is called the option-adjusted spread (OAS).
An embedded option affects the yield that an investor receives from owning a bond. A callable bond is disadvantageous to the investor since
the issuer can terminate the cash flows before maturity. This means that a portion of the additional yield incorporates the option value.
Subtracting that option value compensates for the other risks mentioned above. A put option benefits the investor, so the OAS of the bond will be
greater than its Z-spread.

When determining the appropriate YTM for a risky (ie, nongovernment) bond of a given maturity, the convention is to add an additional

question_en: An analyst has compiled the following data about a bond that has an embedded call option and matures in 8 years: If an option pricing model determines that the value of the embedded call is 208 basis points/year, the option-adjusted spread for the bond (in basis points/year) is closest to:
explanation_en:
A bond with an embedded option trades at a price that reflects both the value of the option and the risk of an otherwise similar bond (ie, same
credit quality, coupon rate, maturity) with no embedded option.
An embedded call is a disadvantage to a bondholder since the call can be exercised by the issuer when market conditions are favorable. Thus,
issuers must offer callable bonds with higher yields (implied by the benchmark rate + Z-spread) than the yields required by investors for
comparable bonds with no embedded option (implied by the benchmark rate + OAS). The difference between those bonds is the presence of the
option, and the difference in their spreads is the value of the option (Z-spread − OAS = option value).
To calculate the OAS of a bond, subtract the call option value (in basis points/year) from the Z-spread (eg, 760 − 208 = 552 basis points).

question_en: The I-spread is most appropriately defined as the difference between a bond's yield and:
explanation_en:
A yield spread is the difference between a bond's YTM and a benchmark yield. The bond's yield can be expressed as the sum of
the benchmark rate, which represents factors that affect all bonds, and
the spread, which represents factors that are more specific to a bond or issuer.
Different yield spreads result from the use of different benchmarks. Bond yields are often used as a benchmark, but benchmarks can also be
derived from an interest rate swap curve. The I-spread is defined as the spread that a bond earns versus a swap rate of the same tenor.
(Choice B) The spot curve is used to derive the Z-spread, which is a spread applied across the benchmark curve that allows the bond's
discounted cash flows to equal the bond's price.
(Choice C) The excess yield a bond earns over a government bond is the G-spread.

question_en: An analyst is reviewing the term structure of spreads for a group of fixed-rate corporate bonds. The bonds were all issued in the UK and have the same risk profile. The analyst would most appropriately use the:
explanation_en:
The G-spread, I-spread, and Z-spread are each used to compare the risk of a bond (or bonds with the same risk profile) to that of a benchmark.
However, the:
G-spread is the spread of a bond's YTM over a government benchmark YTM and differs for each time-to-maturity.
I-spread is the spread of a bond's YTM over an interbank lending benchmark rate and differs for each time-to-maturity.
Z-spread is the spread of a bond cash flow's discount rate over a government or interbank lending benchmark spot rate and is the same for
all times-to-maturity.
Since the G-spread and I-spread differ across times-to-maturity, they both reflect the term structure of spreads for bonds with the same risk
profile and different times-to-maturity. Therefore, an analyst interested in comparing how the risk differs across times-to-maturity for bonds with
the same risk profile would use the G-spread or I-spread.
The benchmark used for fixed-rate bonds in the UK, US, and Japan is the G-spread. The I-spread is used to price Euro-denominated corporate
bonds. Since the bonds in this scenario are fixed-rate UK-issued bonds, the G-spread is most appropriate, not the I-spread (Choice A).
The Z-spread (ie, zero-volatility spread) is the constant yield spread that—when added to the benchmark spot rates (not YTMs as with the G- and
I-spreads) and used to discount each bond cash flow—equates the present value of the cash flows with the bond's observed price. The Z-spread
is the same for all times-to-maturity. Therefore, it does not reflect the difference in YTM above the benchmark (and thus the difference in risk)
associated with differences in times-to-maturity (ie, the term structure of spreads) (Choice B).

and 4%. Based on the Z-spread of 6%, the bond's price is calculated as:
(Choice B) 92.92 is the result of incorrectly reversing the 1 and 2 year benchmark spot rates in determining the discount rate for each cash flow.
(Choice C) 98.17 is the result of discounting both cash flows by only the Z-spread, and not adding in the benchmark spot rates to obtain the

question_en: A callable corporate bond's option-adjusted spread (OAS) is most likely calculated using the value (in basis points per year) of the embedded option and the:
explanation_en:
Options embedded in callable bonds complicate comparisons with other bonds. Adjusting the market price of callable bonds for the value of
embedded options makes it easier to assess the impact of other risk factors (eg, credit quality, liquidity) on relative value. For this analysis, the
option-adjusted spread (OAS) is estimated by subtracting the value of the option (in basis points per year) from a bond's Z-spread.
The Z-spread is the constant spread to a benchmark (ie, government or swap) curve that results in a series of periodic discount rates that equate
the present value of a bond's cash flows to its market price. Discount rates based on a Z-spread capture all risks affecting price, including any
embedded options. An option pricing model estimates how much narrower the Z-spread would be for an equivalent noncallable bond. The
callable bond's OAS is used to calculate an option-adjusted price and yield, allowing better comparisons with other securities.
(Choices A and C) The G- and I-spreads are based on the difference between a bond's YTM and a benchmark rate of the same maturity (eg, 5-
year corporate bond versus a 5-year government bond or swap). Since these spreads are computed separately for each maturity, they widen as
maturities increase, reflecting the greater relative risk of corporate securities for longer time horizons.

An analyst gathers the following information on 10-year government benchmark rates (with YTMs assuming semiannual compounding):

| Government bond | 4.18% |
| Interest rate swap | 4.28% |

For a 6% coupon semiannual pay corporate bond with 10 years to maturity and priced at 100.35, the g-spread in basis points (bps) is closest to:
explanation_en:
HP 12c TI BA II Plus
Yield curves display the term structure of interest rates by graphing the relationship between maturities and bond yields. Many governments,
including those of the UK, US, and Japan, regularly issue bonds with select maturities (eg, 2, 5, 10, and 30 years). These benchmark bonds form
the basis of the government yield curve.
The g-spread is the difference between the YTM of a nongovernment bond relative to the YTM of a benchmark government bond with the
same maturity. It quantifies the additional yield (ie, spread) required by the market to own the riskier bond.
In this question, the YTM of the corporate bond can be derived from the information provided using a financial calculator. Stated on a semiannual
basis, the government bond's YTM is 4.18%, and the corporate bond's YTM is 5.95%. Therefore, the g-spread is 0.0595 − 0.0418 = 0.0177, or
177 bps.
(Choice A) 160 bps (0.0595 − 0.0435 = 0.0160) is the difference between the YTM of the bond and the spot rate. It results from an inappropriate
application of the Z-spread concept, which requires the entire benchmark curve's spot rates, not just a single period's YTM.
(Choice B) 167 bps (0.0595 − 0.0428 = 0.0167) is the difference between the YTM of the bond and the benchmark swap rate, or i-spread.

question_en:
An analyst has compiled the following data to analyze a bond:

| 5-year interbank lending rate | 4.83 |

If the bond is five years from maturity, trades at 78.3, and has a 6% annual coupon, paid semiannually, the I-spread for the bond is closest to:
explanation_en:
HP 12c TI BA II Plus
The I-spread is the difference between the yield-to-maturity (YTM) of a given bond and the interbank lending benchmark rate with the same
time-to-maturity. A benchmark rate is a broad market measure that reflects macroeconomic risk factors. The I-spread over different times-to-
maturity indicates the term structure of spreads since the spreads differ across times-to-maturity.
To determine the I-spread of a bond, the YTM of the bond should be calculated first. In this scenario:
The periodicity (m) of the bond is 2 since the coupons are semiannual.
The number of periods is therefore 10 = (m × n = 2 × 5).
The periodic coupon payment is 3 = [(0.06 ÷ 2) × 100] since the bond's annual coupon is 6%, paid semiannually.
The present value is the price of the bond, 78.3.
The periodic discount rate is determined, using a financial calculator, according to the following formula:
The periodicity of the bond is 2, so multiplying the periodic discount rate (r) by 2 will determine the annual YTM: YTM = r × m = 5.94 × 2 = 11.88%.
The I-spread is the difference between the YTM of the bond and the interbank lending benchmark rate with the same time-to-maturity, 4.83%.
Therefore, the I-spread is 11.88 − 4.83 = 7.05%

The bond with the greatest effective annual rate is most likely:
explanation_en:
Bonds with different periodicities can be directly compared by converting all yields to an effective annual rate (EAR). The EAR is equal to the YTM with a periodicity of 1. A bond that pays only once per year (periodicity = 1) has an EAR equal to its stated annual rate; a bond that pays more often (periodicity > 1) has a higher EAR than its stated annual rate, since more frequent compounding increases the EAR.

Bond X: (1 + 0.09/2)^2 = (1 + YTM1)^1 => YTM1 = (1 + 0.09/2)^2 - 1 = 0.092 (9.2%)
Bond Y: no conversion needed, periodicity already 1 => YTM1 = 0.09 (9.0%)
Bond Z: (1 + 0.09/4)^4 = (1 + YTM1)^1 => YTM1 = (1 + 0.09/4)^4 - 1 = 0.0931 (9.31%)

Bond Z has the greatest effective annual rate (9.31%).

question_en: A government spot-rate curve is shown below: If a 3-year, 5% annual-pay nongovernment bond has a zero-volatility spread of 55 basis points and a par value of 100, the highest arbitrage-free price that an investor should be willing to pay for the bond (per 100 par value) is closest to:
explanation_en:
HP 12c TI BA II Plus
A bond's no-arbitrage (ie, arbitrage-free) value is calculated by discounting each cash flow by the spot rate corresponding to when that cash
flow occurs. Since spot rates are derived from a yield curve for government bonds, which are default-free, the rates do not reflect a
nongovernment bond's credit risk. Therefore, the no-arbitrage value is, in general, higher than the bond's market price.
To equate a bond's arbitrage-free price with its market price, an identical extra yield called the zero-volatility spread (ie, Z-spread) is added to each
spot rate. The Z-spread reflects the additional compensation needed for the risks of investing in a nongovernment bond. This means that the
appropriate discount rate for each cash flow is the applicable spot rate plus the Z-spread, as shown below:
(Choice A) 95.90 results from discounting each cash flow by 0.0655, which is the sum of the 3-year spot rate and the 55-basis-point Z-spread.
(Choice C) 97.50 results from discounting each cash flow at its applicable spot rate but neglecting to add the Z-spread to each rate.

question_en: A floating-rate note has a quoted margin of 35 basis points (bps) and a discount margin of −15 bps. If the relevant reference rate is 3.25% on the bond's reset date, the new coupon rate is most likely:
explanation_en:
The coupon rate of a floating-rate note (ie, FRN or floater) is based on a reference rate (eg, LIBOR). The quoted margin is the yield that is
added to the reference rate to determine each period's coupon rate. The quoted margin typically does not change during the life of the bond. The
coupon rate of the FRN in this scenario is the LIBOR rate plus 35 basis points (bps), or 3.25% + 0.35% = 3.60%.
The discount margin of an FRN (also called the required margin) is an adjustment to the rate used to discount the bond's cash flows. The
discount margin represents the additional yield required given the risks of an FRN. When the bond is issued, the discount margin is the same as
the quoted margin, but changes in the bond's risks cause the discount margin to change. Any change in the discount margin affects the bond's
present value, not its coupon rate.
(Choice A) 3.10% results from adding the discount margin (−15 bps), rather than the quoted margin, to the reference rate.
(Choice C) 3.45% results from inappropriately adding the sum of the quoted margin and discount margin (20 bps) to the reference rate.

question_en: A 4%, annual-pay bond is currently priced at 105 per 100 of par value. It has three years to maturity and is callable at a price of 102.5 at the end of Year 1 and 100.5 at the end of Year 2. The yield-to-worst is the bond's:
explanation_en:
A bond's present value is calculated by discounting its expected cash flows using its required return (ie, YTM). One of the assumptions underlying
YTM is that the bond is held to maturity; however, this assumption may not always hold for callable bonds, which the issuer can redeem before
their scheduled maturity.
Once called, a bond has no future cash flows, so its yield is calculated as though it will be called on its call date, with the call price substituted for
its face value. For bonds with multiple call dates, a separate yield is calculated for each date, and each yield is referred to as the yield to first call,
yield to second call, etc. The yield-to-worst is the lowest yield for all possible call dates as well as the YTM.
The bond in this question can be called at the end of Year 1 or Year 2. Each yield-to-call can be computed using a financial calculator. The
calculator strokes are shown below. The bond's yield to first call of 1.43%, which is the lowest of the three possible yields, is its yield-to-worst.
(Choice A) 2.26% is the bond's yield to maturity.
(Choice C) 1.68% is the bond's yield to second call.

question_en: A bond's current price is 95 per 100 par value. Its current yield is best described as its annual coupon payments divided by its:
explanation_en: The current yield is the total of one year's coupon payments divided by the bond's flat price. The flat price is the quoted price, which excludes any accrued interest. Current yield as a return measure is advantageous because it is quick and easy to calculate. In this scenario, the bond has a 6% semiannual coupon, so there are 2 coupon payments of 3 (ie, 3% of 100 par) per year. The current yield is calculated as: As a rate of return measure for an investor, current yield is a very rough approximation since current yield does not account for: any capital appreciation in the bond's price; or any accrued interest paid by the investor at purchase; or the compounding effect of the frequency of coupon payments. (Choice B) 6.3% is the bond's current yield at the time of the bond purchase, based on the price of 95 per 100 par value. (Choice C) 6.5% is the bond's yield-to-maturity based on a price of 99.
